Neonates of the West African slender-snouted crocodile emerge after an incubation period of approximately 95 days [ab = approximately 95 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], a duration that falls within the typical range for medium-bodied crocodylians. At hatching, these juveniles measure about 32.5 cm [Lb = about 32.5 cm] in total length, a modest size that reflects the constraints of the parchment-shelled egg from which they emerge. Each hatchling begins life with an initial wet weight of 104.7 grams [Ww0 = 104.7 grams], a mass that is heavily dependent on yolk reserves carried over from the embryonated egg. This early-life body mass is modest relative to the adult dimensions the animal will eventually attain, underscoring the dramatic shift in trophic ecology that accompanies the transition from yolk-sac larva to active forager. Field surveys in Ivory Coast have documented that clutches typically number between 7 and 22 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 7 and 22 eggs per clutch], and females are thought to produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] under the prevailing thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], a reproductive tempo that aligns with the slow life-history strategy characteristic of many tropical crocodylians.

Sexual maturation in this species is a protracted process, particularly for females, who typically require 12.5 years after hatching [tp = 12.5 years after hatching] to reach puberty under average conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended juvenile phase, during which individuals function as immature sub-adults, is likely an adaptation to the competitive environment of riverine systems where large body size confers a substantial advantage in both prey capture and social dominance. The attainment of sexual maturity in females is closely tied to achieving a total length at puberty of approximately 2 meters [Lp = approximately 2 meters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonadal activation and the ability to produce a first egg clutch. For males, growth trajectories differ markedly, with puberty also associated with a similar body length, though reliable field data specific to male maturation remain sparse. This size-based trigger for reproductive activation is common among crocodylians and ensures that only individuals with sufficient somatic reserves can channel energy toward the energetically demanding process of nesting and egg production.

Adult body size in Mecistops cataphractus exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature common among crocodylians where males outgrow females considerably. Females reach an ultimate total length of approximately 250 cm [Li = approximately 250 cm], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of around 68.5 kilograms [Wwi = around 68.5 kilograms]. Males, in contrast, attain a substantially larger ultimate total length of about 420 cm [Li = about 420 cm], with an associated ultimate wet weight of roughly 325 kilograms [Wwi = roughly 325 kilograms]. This divergence in adult size likely reflects differential selective pressures acting on each sex: larger males secure greater access to breeding territories and mating opportunities, while female body size is constrained by the energetic costs of egg production and nest attendance. The growth trajectories that produce these ultimate sizes are influenced by resource availability and temperature, with captive-reared individuals often reaching these asymptotic values more rapidly than their wild counterparts, which must contend with seasonal prey fluctuations and intraspecific competition.

Longevity data for the West African slender-snouted crocodile remain limited, but available records from captive populations indicate that the maximum lifespan for this species is approximately 56.1 years [am = approximately 56.1 years] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This substantial lifespan, which is among the longest documented for crocodylians of its body size, reflects a life-history strategy characterized by delayed reproduction, iteroparous breeding, and low adult mortality in the absence of significant predation. The extended period of reproductive viability allows females to produce multiple clutches across several decades, thereby compensating for the relatively modest annual fecundity of a single clutch per year. Senescence in this species is poorly documented, but older individuals in captivity show signs of reduced mobility and dental wear, which may limit their ability to capture large prey in the wild and ultimately contribute to natural mortality as age-related physiological decline progresses.

The nesting ecology of the slender-snouted crocodile is closely tied to the seasonal hydrology of West African river basins. Gravid females construct mound nests from riverine vegetation and mud, typically during the dry season when water levels recede, exposing suitable nesting banks. The leathery-shelled eggs deposited within these mounds are subjected to the ambient thermal conditions of the decomposing plant material, which can buffer against extreme temperatures and maintain a relatively stable incubation environment. At the average incubation temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], though the precise number of eggs per nesting event varies considerably with female body condition and local prey abundance. Hatchling survival is low during the first year due to predation by fish, waterbirds, and larger crocodiles, a demographic bottleneck that shapes the population's overall size structure and reinforces the selective advantage of attaining a larger body size as rapidly as possible during the juvenile phase.
